sources.title: M. Seckler, S. Heinz, J. A. Bargas-Avila, K. Opwis and A. N. Tuch, Designing usable web forms: empirical evaluation of web form improvement guidelines, Proceedings of CHI 2014, pp. 1275–1284
sources.access_level: Full text (methods and results) checked via author PDF https://research.google.com/pubs/archive/42513.pdf and an author-uploaded copy
supported_claims: Between-subject study with 65 participants (32 original, 33 improved) on three reconstructed real-world registration forms.
Improvements were applied as a bundle derived from 20 web-form guidelines.
Mean completion time fell from 113 to 85 s (Sueddeutsche) and 105 to 70 s (NZZ), both significant; Spiegel fell from 104 to 85 s without a significant time difference.
Improved versions needed fewer submission trials for all three forms; satisfaction effects varied by form and scale.
limitations: Bundled intervention: no isolated feature effect can be attributed.
Registration forms differ from image-metadata transcription.

sources.title: J. A. Bargas-Avila, S. Orsini, H. Piosczyk, D. Urwyler and K. Opwis, Enhancing online forms: Use format specifications for fields with format restrictions to help respondents, Interacting with Computers, 23(1), 33–39, 2011
supported_claims: Experiment with 166 participants across four advance format-guidance conditions.
Giving format details in advance reduced errors and submission trials.
An explicit rule was the most efficient presentation; adding an example gave no further benefit.
limitations: Abstract verified only; no effect sizes are reported in this report.
Does not show that an added example is harmful.

sources.title: M. Seckler, A. N. Tuch, K. Opwis and J. A. Bargas-Avila, User-friendly locations of error messages in web forms: Put them on the right side of the erroneous input field, Interacting with Computers, 24(3), 107–118, 2012
supported_claims: Study with 303 participants comparing six error-message locations.
Messages near the erroneous field gave better performance than top or bottom placement.
The right-hand location was rated most satisfying and intuitive.
limitations: Abstract verified only; no effect sizes used.
Concerns message location, not validation timing.
Prototype layout was not tested against this result.

sources.title: A. A. Zeleke et al., Evaluation of Electronic and Paper-Pen Data Capturing Tools for Data Quality in a Public Health Survey in a Health and Demographic Surveillance Site, Ethiopia: Randomized Controlled Crossover Health Care Information Technology Evaluation, JMIR mHealth and uHealth, 7(2), e10995, 2019
supported_claims: Randomized crossover evaluation: 12 interviewers collected 1246 questionnaires with each method in paired simultaneous interviews with randomized tool order.
Overall item error rate was 1.67% on paper and 0.60% electronically.
Questionnaires with at least one error: 41.89% paper vs 30.89% electronic.
Electronic ODK forms used number, date and skip checks, were editable, and required only identifiers.
limitations: Indirect: clinical survey context with a paper comparator, not a browser table.
Effect cannot be assigned to one UI mechanism.
1246 questionnaires are not 1246 independent interface users.

sources.title: K. Nakamura, Y. Kasahara, G. Miura, A. Kinoshita and T. Asao, Usability of Two Clinical Registry Data-Entry Interfaces: A Randomized Crossover Study, Informatics, 13(10), 171, 2026
sources.access_level: Early-access abstract only, via publisher page https://www.mdpi.com/2227-9709/13/10/171 (published 14 October 2026); full methods/results not verified
supported_claims: Within-participant randomized crossover study with 20 therapists on simulated registry tasks.
The tested wizard interface was associated with shorter times, fewer errors and lower NASA-TLX workload.
Authors caution against concluding general wizard superiority.
limitations: Navigation and input methods also differed between interfaces.
Cautious supporting evidence only, not central proof.

sources.title: J. A. Bargas-Avila, G. Oberholzer, P. Schmutz, M. de Vito and K. Opwis, Usable error message presentation in the World Wide Web: Do not show errors right away, Interacting with Computers, 19(3), 330–341, 2007
supported_claims: Two studies with 77 and 90 undergraduate participants using forms with artificial, undisclosed format obstacles.
In the second study, mean repeated errors were 3.48 (all errors after submit), 3.17 (one at a time after submit) and 7.25 (on blur); overall difference p < .03.
No significant completion-time differences were found.
limitations: Undisclosed obstacles differ from this schema, which shows rules in advance.
Supports testing save-time initial validation, not a universal optimal timing.
